summary:
**Agnidrishti** ("See the fire. Verify the signal.") is a web app built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, responding to the challenge "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots."

**The problem:** Satellites detect fires differently. MODIS and VIIRS record hotspots at very different scales, with VIIRS averaging 8.27 detections per district-day against roughly 0.5 for MODIS. So when recorded fire activity changes over time, it's hard to tell whether the landscape really changed or whether the observing satellite did.

**The solution:** Agnidrishti processes real NASA FIRMS data from 2012 to 2026 for three high-fire districts in Nepal: Banke, Bardiya and Chitwan. A Python pipeline keeps the five sensors separate, then tests three correction methods (ratio, quantile mapping and shrinkage) on held-out years. An independent audit rechecks the results and grades how reliable each one is. The React and TypeScript frontend presents everything through an explorable weekly fire calendar, plus a methodology page showing the validation results.

**Scientific honesty:** The project reports its limits openly. The comparison of correction methods was inconclusive, so no winner is declared and the harmonized data is labelled provisional. VIIRS is treated as a reference scale rather than ground truth, detections are hotspots rather than unique fires, and missing observations are never counted as zero.
details:
Tagline: See the fire. Verify the signal.
Challenge: NASA Space Apps 2026, Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots

1. The problem

NASA’s fire-detection satellites do not all see fire the same way. MODIS (on Terra and Aqua) detects at a 1 km pixel size, while VIIRS (on Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21) detects at 375 m. VIIRS therefore picks up many more, smaller hotspots. In our study districts it recorded roughly 14 to 17 times more detections than MODIS on the same days.

This creates a trap. When the data shifts from one sensor to another, fire activity can appear to jump, even though the landscape has not changed. Anyone reading a long fire record, such as a researcher, a forest office or a journalist, can mistake a change in the instrument for a change in the fires.

2. What Agnidrishti does

Agnidrishti is a satellite-aware fire activity calendar that shows what each satellite recorded, how much to trust it, and what a harmonized view looks like. It answers one question: did fire activity change, or did the way we observe it change?

It is built on four principles:

  • Missing is never zero. A day with no observation is shown as missing, not as “no fires”.
  • VIIRS is a reference scale, not ground truth. Harmonizing to VIIRS makes records comparable but does not make them correct.
  • A detection is not a fire. One fire can produce many detections, and false alarms occur.
  • Uncertainty is shown wherever a number is shown.

3. Study areas and data

  • Source: NASA FIRMS Standard Processing data.
  • Platforms: MODIS Terra, MODIS Aqua, VIIRS Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. They are kept separate from start to finish and never merged early.
  • Coverage: January to June 2012 through 2026, plus July 2026, for high-fire districts in Nepal (Banke, Bardiya and Chitwan in the published build, with further regions added). These are selected study areas, not a ranking of Nepal’s most fire-affected districts.
  • Boundaries: OCHA COD-AB administrative boundaries. Each detection is assigned to a district by exact point-in-polygon matching, with no bounding-box shortcut.
  • Provenance: 1,668 download chunks, each checked against a SHA-256 manifest. About 1.02 million raw records reduce to about 124,500 detections inside the districts.
  • Products: 0.1° grid cell-days and daily and ISO-week summaries. Near-real-time data is stored separately from the final processed data.

4. Method

Coverage first. Before any correction, every day and sensor is classified with a six-state vocabulary: observed, insufficient, incomplete, missing, not requested or unavailable. This keeps “no data” from being mistaken for “no fire”.

Three correction methods, each fitted only on training years:

  1. Ratio correction, using district-month ratios with documented fallbacks.
  2. Quantile mapping, which preserves zeros and caps values at the range seen in training.
  3. Monthly shrinkage, which blends each month’s ratio with the district ratio, weighted by how much data that month has.

Validation:

  • Whole years (2019 and 2022) are held out, with a 30-day purge gap, so test data never sits next to training data.
  • All methods are scored on the identical sample.
  • Metrics include MAE, RMSE, log-RMSE, bias, Pearson correlation and Lin’s concordance correlation (CCC), with moving-block bootstrap confidence intervals.

Extra checks:

  • A Seam Audit looks at the step between sensors before and after correction.
  • A Lights-Out Backtest hides a period and checks whether the seasonal pattern is recovered.
  • An independent audit recomputes the metrics with separate code.
  • Leave-one-year-out testing and reliability strata grade how much each district-month can be trusted.

5. Results

  • Scale gap: on validation days, VIIRS averaged 8.27 detections per district-day against 0.49 for Terra and 0.58 for Aqua.
  • Method comparison: shrinkage (CCC 0.625), ratio (0.620) and quantile mapping (0.516). The evidence does not separate the three, so we declare no winning method.
  • Seam Audit: the sensor step shrinks from roughly 8 to 50 times before correction to about 0.8 to 2.1 after. This is a diagnostic, not proof of cause, and some residual step remains.
  • Temporal robustness: leave-one-year-out CCC ranges from 0.37 to 0.71, with no year falling below our caution floor.
  • Reliability: 2 district-month cells are graded reliable, 4 caution, 15 insufficient and 15 unavailable.
  • Weak spot: Chitwan has the lowest agreement (CCC 0.19 to 0.34), and this is carried into every view.

6. The application

  • Explorer: choose a district, year and product, and see a weekly calendar. Unobserved periods are hatched, and detail for each week is one click away.
  • Map: district context with a clear caption that it shows detection areas, not fire locations.
  • Methodology page: the methods, validation design and live results.
  • Design: the interface keeps raw and corrected views visibly separate and never shows an unobserved period as zero.

7. Limitations (stated openly)

  • Harmonization is a provisional correction. It reduces, but does not remove, the sensor gap.
  • Daily agreement is moderate. Weekly summaries are the more useful scale.
  • August to December were not requested, so those months are out of scope, not zero.
  • Detections are not unique fires and are not ground truth.
  • Only a small number of district-months reach “reliable” status.
  • No claim is made about NASA endorsement or about operational or policy use.

8. Relevance and impact

Suomi NPP stopped delivering new fire data on 2 November 2026, so the record is moving to NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. Making records from different instruments comparable, with honest uncertainty, is now a practical need for researchers, environmental groups and forest authorities. Agnidrishti offers a transparent worked example. It makes no claim to replace official systems such as ICIMOD’s Forest Fire Detection and Monitoring System or Nepal’s BIPAD portal.

9. Technology

React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind and React Router on the frontend, and a Python 3.11 pipeline (numpy and shapely) with 76 automated tests. The site is static, so it needs no server and its results are reproducible from the hashed data.

10. Roadmap (not yet built)

  • A Community Fire Context view with plain-language local summaries.
  • A Fire Activity Outlook estimating the chance of above-normal satellite detections, shown only if it passes pre-registered validation gates.
